title: Chebyshev Nodes: Optimal Interpolation Points
content: The k-th Chebyshev node of degree n is cos((2k+1)π/(2n)) for k = 0, …, n−1. These are the roots of the Chebyshev polynomial Tₙ(x) = cos(n·arccos(x)). Their defining property is that they minimize the maximum interpolation error among all choices of n nodes in [−1, 1]: for any polynomial of degree ≤ n−1 interpolating f at these nodes, the error is bounded by ‖f‖/(2^{n−1}·n!). The theorem chebyshevNode_mem_Icc proves they lie in [−1, 1] using |cos| ≤ 1, which follows from neg_one_le_cos and cos_le_one.
mathContext: $x_k^{(n)} = \cos\left(\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n}\right)$ for $k = 0,\ldots,n-1$; these are roots of $T_n(x) = \cos(n \arccos x)$; $x_k^{(n)} \in [-1,1]$

title: Injectivity of Chebyshev Nodes via Strict Monotonicity of Cosine
content: chebyshevNodes_injective proves that the n Chebyshev nodes are distinct. The key is that cos is strictly decreasing on [0, π] (Real.strictAntiOn_cos), and all arguments (2k+1)π/(2n) lie in (0, π) ⊆ [0, π]. The proof shows equal cosine values imply equal arguments (by strictAntiOn.injOn), then equal k indices by field_simp + linarith on the linear equation 2k₁+1 = 2k₂+1. The distinctness is essential: if nodes coincide, the Lagrange basis polynomials are undefined (division by zero in (xₖ − xᵢ)).

title: Lagrange Interpolation at Chebyshev Nodes
content: The Lagrange basis polynomial ℓₖ(x) = ∏_{i≠k} (x − xᵢ)/(xₖ − xᵢ) satisfies ℓₖ(xₖ) = 1 and ℓₖ(xᵢ) = 0 for i ≠ k. The Lagrange interpolation polynomial 𝓛ⁿf(x) = Σₖ f(xₖ) ℓₖ(x) is the unique polynomial of degree ≤ n−1 agreeing with f at all n nodes. The definition uses Finset.univ.erase k for the product over i ≠ k. chebyshevInterp specializes this to Chebyshev nodes. Note: lagrangeBasis is referenced from the Erdős #1153 formalization, demonstrating code reuse across related gallery entries.
mathContext: $\ell_k(x) = \prod_{i \neq k} \frac{x - x_i}{x_k - x_i}$; $\mathcal{L}^n f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k) \ell_k(x)$; $\mathcal{L}^n f$ is the unique polynomial of degree $\leq n-1$ through $(x_k, f(x_k))$

title: Limit Points: Topological Foundation
content: IsLimitPoint seq y means y is arbitrarily well approximated by seq for arbitrarily large indices — this is the ε-δ definition of a limit point (also called 'cluster point' or 'accumulation point'). The set limitPointSet seq collects all such y. The key theorem limitPointSet_isClosed proves that for bounded sequences, this set is closed. Proof: the complement is open — if y is not a limit point, there exists ε > 0 and N such that seq is ε-away from y for all n ≥ N; any z within ε/2 of y is also not a limit point by the reverse triangle inequality. This closedness is crucial: the Erdős conjecture asserts every closed set can arise as a limit point set.
mathContext: $y \in \text{limitPointSet}(a_n) \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \forall N,\; \exists n \geq N: |a_n - y| < \varepsilon$; $\text{limitPointSet}(a_n)$ is closed for bounded sequences

title: Axiom: Erdős's 1941 Divergence Result
content: erdos_1941_divergence axiomatizes Erdős's 1941 theorem: for x = cos(πp/q) with odd p, q, there exists a continuous f whose Chebyshev interpolation values diverge to ∞. This was a shocking result at the time — Chebyshev nodes were expected to give good interpolation for smooth functions, but Erdős showed divergence is possible even at rational-cosine points. The axiom parameterizes p, q as positive odd naturals and constructs x via cos. The condition that p, q are odd ensures x = cos(πp/q) is not itself a Chebyshev node of any degree (which would give trivial convergence).
mathContext: $x = \cos(\pi p/q)$, $p, q$ odd $\Rightarrow$ $\exists f \in C[-1,1]: \mathcal{L}^n f(x) \to \infty$ along a subsequence

title: The Open Conjecture: Any Closed Set Is Realizable
content: erdos_1151_conjecture is the open problem: for any x ∈ [−1, 1] and any closed A ⊆ [−1, 1], there exists a continuous f such that limitPointSet(𝓛ⁿf(x)) = A exactly. This would give a complete topological classification of the limit-point behaviors of Lagrange interpolation at Chebyshev nodes — any closed set, however complicated, can appear. The axiom states this as an existence result parameterized by x, A, and their containment conditions. Erdős claimed this without proof in a 1943 note; it was listed as open by Vértesi in 1999.
mathContext: $\forall x \in [-1,1],\; \forall A \subseteq [-1,1]$ closed, $\exists f \in C[-1,1]: \text{limitPointSet}(\mathcal{L}^n f(x)) = A$

title: Special Cases: Convergence and Dense Orbit
content: Two special cases are derived from the conjecture as immediate corollaries. erdos_1151_convergent_case takes A = {y}: the limit point set is a singleton, meaning 𝓛ⁿf(x) converges to y. erdos_1151_dense_case takes A = [−1, 1]: the limit point set is the full interval, meaning the sequence visits every point arbitrarily closely (a 'topologically chaotic' orbit). Both proofs are one-liners that apply the axiom with the correct closedness witnesses: isClosed_singleton for {y} and isClosed_Icc for [−1, 1]. These cases bound the spectrum from 'completely convergent' to 'completely divergent' behavior.
